docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:442:<p>In his essay on the nature of phonological prosodic typology, Hyman (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B37">2012</xref>) states that &#8220;phonological typology does not consist in the comparison of surface inventories, whether of surface consonants and vowels or tags such as L+H and H*L&#8221; (p. 230). Our view is different. Both phonological and broad phonetic comparison can offer important insights. It may be useful to know, for instance, in what languages /d/ is palatalized to [&#676;] in contact with palatal vowels, realized as an approximant [&#240;] or as a flap [&#638;] in contexts of lenition, or devoiced to [t] word-finally.</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:445:<p>A reviewer points out that it is possible to compare across intonational grammars of languages, even without a common understanding of the meaning of labels. It is certainly possible, but the task is rendered more difficult.</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:448:<p>At the practical level, it is also difficult for, say, a teacher of Spanish phonetics for native speakers of American English to know what to include in the syllabus in a unit on intonation, as important differences between the two languages that a student would have to learn (beyond differences in the nuclear stress rule, where differences can be more clearly stated).</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:454:<p>Note that one of the languages included in Table <xref ref-type="table" rid="T1">1</xref>, standard Neo-&#352;tokavian Serbian/Croatian/Bosnian, has lexical pitch accent. This, however, does not necessarily affect the notation of boundary tones.</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:457:<p>The same argument for broad phonetic transcription applies, of course, to the segmental level. In WALS (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B51">Maddieson, 2013</xref>), for instance, Spanish is listed as a language with only voiceless stops /p t k/, because the voiced obstruents, which have both noncontinuant [b d g] and noncontinuant [&#946; &#240; &#611;] allophones (or more exactly a continuum of degrees of constriction), are analyzed as /&#946; &#240; &#611;/ by the author, whereas Catalan and Basque, which have essentially the same allophony, are said to oppose /p t k/ to /b d g/. Arguably, for comparative purposes it is more illuminating to note that in Spanish, Catalan, and Basque, in some contexts, including intervocalically, [&#946; &#240; &#611;] are typically found instead of [b d g], which are found after a pause, whereas Brazilian Portuguese, for instance does not have this allophony. Analysis at the phonological level is a more complicated matter, and different authors may choose to represent Sp. [ka&#240;a] as either /kada/ or /ka&#240;a/ depending on considerations of system symmetry and frequency across contexts.</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:466:<p>The only case where agreement was not reached was for the Argentinean Spanish early rise, which has the shape shown in Figure <xref ref-type="fig" rid="F2">2</xref> (right panel) and Figure <xref ref-type="fig" rid="F3">3</xref> (leftmost panel). In Prieto and Roseano (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B58">2010</xref>), this pitch accent was transcribed as L+H*+L only for this particular dialect.</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:469:<p>We should note some systematic differences in the realization of the L*+H pitch accent label across Romance languages (see the chapters in <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B24">Frota &amp; Prieto&#8217;s, 2015, book</xref>). While in languages such as Catalan, Spanish, and Romanian, the turning point of the L*+H pitch accent is aligned with the end of the accented syllable, in Italian and Portuguese it is aligned before the end of the accented vowel (with variation across varieties between the first third and the second third of the vowel in Portuguese). Importantly, prosodic labels should be broad enough to encompass these differences in realization, just as in segmental IPA transcription where, for instance, [t] means &#8216;voiceless dental, alveolar or postalveolar plosive&#8217;, without specifying other features where languages may differ.</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:472:<p>In more recent versions of Sp_ToBI the diacritic to indicate displacement has been changed to &lt;, as in other ToBI systems. That is, this pitch accent is now noted as L+&lt;H* (see <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B36">Hualde &amp; Prieto, 2015</xref>).</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:475:<p>Together with Sun-Ah Jun, the authors of this paper organized a <italic>Workshop on Developing an International Prosodic Alphabet</italic> (IPrA) within the AM framework as a satellite meeting of the <italic>18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences</italic> (ICPhS, August 2015). The main aim of the workshop was to present the motivation for an international set of symbols (e.g., the IPrA inventory) to be used for the transcription of intonational contours and prosodic structure across languages, as well as an initial proposal of IPrA inventory for pitch accents, boundary tones, and non-<italic>F<sub>0</sub></italic> features (see <ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="http://www.linguistics.ucla.edu/ipra_workshop/Proposals.htm">http://www.linguistics.ucla.edu/ipra_workshop/Proposals.htm</ext-link>). The idea was discussed among more than 80 prosody researchers, and it was decided that two more workshops could take place in 2016. A team of prosody experts that have worked in typologically diverse languages and on diverse areas (prosodic contact, prosodic development, and automatic analysis of corpora) will be responsible for developing the IPrA proposal for pitch accents, boundary tones, and non-<italic>F<sub>0</sub></italic> features.</p>
docs/evidence/source-snapshots/labphon-11-ipra.jats.xml:481:<p>The language data come from the two volumes on prosodic typology edited by Sun-Ah Jun (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B40">Jun, 2005</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B41">2014</xref>) and the volume on Romance languages edited by Frota and Prieto (<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="B24">2015</xref>).</p></fn>
